opus-5.5.text:
I think the complexity comes from the fact that you're not really building one thing. When people say "general-purpose model," it sounds like a single artifact, but in practice it's a whole system of interlocking problems, and every one of them can become the bottleneck at any given time.

At the most basic level there are three layers you have to get right simultaneously. The first is compute and infrastructure: how you organize thousands of chips, keep training stable over weeks or months, and recover when something breaks at 3 a.m. The second is data: not just how much you have, but its distribution, its quality, and how you mix it. The third is the algorithm and the training recipe. What makes it hard is that these three aren't independent. A small change in the data mixture can change what the optimal architecture looks like. An infrastructure constraint can rule out an algorithm that would otherwise be better. So you're optimizing a coupled system, and you can't just hand each piece to a separate team and stitch the results together at the end.

The second source of complexity is that "general" means you can't define success with one metric. If you build a model for a single task, you know what to optimize. With a general model you care about reasoning, coding, long context, writing, multilingual ability, safety, and so on. These capabilities sometimes reinforce each other and sometimes compete. A lot of the real craft is in managing those trade-offs: deciding what you're willing to sacrifice, and finding the places where one capability unexpectedly lifts several others.

Third, there's a lot of uncertainty that you can only resolve by running experiments at scale, and scale is expensive. Something that works on a small model may not transfer to a large one, and the reverse is also true. So you have to develop a kind of judgment: which small-scale signals you trust, which ones you don't, and when to commit resources to a big run. I'd say that judgment is one of the scarcest things in this field, and it's very hard to write down. It lives in the team.

And finally, the target keeps moving. The paradigm itself has shifted. First it was mostly about scaling pretraining. Then it was about alignment and making the model useful. Now much more of the frontier is about reinforcement learning, reasoning, and agents that can act over long horizons. Each shift changes what the bottleneck is. So the complexity isn't just technical; it's also organizational. You need a team that can keep re-learning and re-prioritizing, rather than locking into the last thing that worked.

So if I had to summarize: building a general model is less like solving one hard problem and more like running an evolving system where everything is coupled, success is multi-dimensional, and the ground keeps moving under you. The teams that do well are the ones that treat it as an end-to-end problem and keep their taste and judgment sharp.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general-purpose model as a system of interlocking problems, but does not say that consolidating capabilities into one model simplifies the surrounding system architecture.

r002.rationale: It identifies the need to support diverse capabilities—including reasoning, coding, long context, writing, and multilingual ability—and says balancing them adds complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the complexity is fundamentally a problem of compressing a lot of things that used to be separate into one system, and then making that system scale.

If you look at how AI worked before large models, every task had its own pipeline. Translation was one model, question answering was another, dialogue was another. The complexity was distributed across many small systems, and each was simple on its own. The shift with general-purpose models is that you push all of that into a single network and a single training process. So the complexity doesn't disappear, it concentrates. Now one system has to hold language, reasoning, world knowledge, code, and the ability to follow instructions, all at once.

That creates a few layers of difficulty. The first is the obvious one, scale. You're coordinating thousands of GPUs, enormous datasets, and a training run that can go on for months. Any small inefficiency gets multiplied. The second layer is data. People talk about compute, but the real bottleneck is often what you feed in. Data quality, data mixing, how much code versus text versus multilingual content, these decisions change the model's character in ways you can't fully predict ahead of time. The third layer is alignment, getting the model to be actually useful and safe for a human rather than just a good next-token predictor.

What makes it genuinely hard is that these layers interact. A decision about data affects how you should scale. A scaling choice affects what alignment can fix later. And you don't get many experiments at full scale, so a lot of the craft is building good small-scale proxies and trusting that they transfer. In a sense the complexity isn't in any single component, it's in the fact that you're making a long chain of irreversible bets with limited feedback.

The way I think about managing that is to keep the principles simple even when the system is big. Scaling laws, clean data, a clear objective. If you let the complexity of the engineering drive the research, you get lost. If you keep a simple picture of what you're optimizing and let the engineering serve that, it stays tractable.

r001.rationale: It contrasts separate task-specific pipelines with one network and training process, communicating the architectural consolidation even as complexity concentrates in that system.

r002.rationale: It says the system must handle language, reasoning, world knowledge, code, and instructions all at once, identifying breadth across scenarios as a source of difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think the complexity comes from the fact that you’re trying to build one system that can handle many different tasks, including tasks you didn’t anticipate. For a specialized system, you can define the objective fairly clearly and optimize toward it. For a general-purpose model, even defining what “better” means is difficult. Does it mean stronger reasoning, broader knowledge, greater reliability, or a better understanding of what the user wants? You need all of those, and progress on one doesn’t necessarily translate into progress on the others.

Then there’s the interaction between data, algorithms, and computing infrastructure. These aren’t independent pieces. A change in the data can affect which training method works best, and an algorithm that looks promising in a small experiment may behave differently at a larger scale. So the challenge isn’t simply making each component better; it’s understanding how the whole system behaves.

That’s why I see it as both a scientific problem and an engineering problem. You need hypotheses about how learning works, but you also need the ability to test those hypotheses reliably. And as the model becomes more capable, you have to keep asking whether your evaluations are measuring the capabilities people actually need.

r001.rationale: The response says one system must handle many tasks, but does not state that consolidating capabilities simplifies the surrounding architecture.

r002.rationale: It identifies handling many different tasks, including unanticipated ones, as a source of complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the complexity comes from the fact that you’re not building a system for one clearly defined task. You want the same model to handle many different tasks, including situations you didn’t anticipate. So the challenge is both to develop general capabilities and to make those capabilities reliable.

There are several layers that interact: the data, the model architecture, the training objective, and the infrastructure. If you change one, you often have to rethink the others. More data, for example, is useful only if the model can learn effectively from it and you have the systems to run the experiments.

And then there’s evaluation. With a specialized system, success can be relatively easy to measure. With a general-purpose model, a good benchmark score captures only part of what you care about. You also need to understand where it fails, whether it can adapt to unfamiliar problems, and whether users can actually depend on it. That makes the whole process a continuous cycle of research, engineering, and learning from real use.

r001.rationale: The response says one model should handle many tasks, but does not state that consolidating capabilities simplifies the surrounding system architecture.

r002.rationale: It identifies handling many different tasks and unanticipated situations as a challenge, directly connecting diverse scenarios to the complexity.
